newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military offers controversial force plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military offers controversial force plan.

text.p: The U.S. military marched into a political minefield on Monday, asking Congress to close more domestic bases but make only small troop cuts while spending billions on weapons for the 21st century.

Despite strong opposition from lawmakers, President Bill Clinton quickly supported the proposal that would batter the pocketbooks of American communities by adding to the 98 big domestic bases already being closed after the Cold War.

Defence Secretary William Cohen unveiled the plan at a news conference, pressing Congress to okay two rounds of base closings at home in 1999 and 2001 to save money for jets and other arms, while paring just 61,700 troops from the 1.4 million-member armed forces.

The Quadrennial Defence Review, or "QDR" as the proposal is known, has already drawn sharp criticism from Democrats and Republicans in Congress because it seeks sensitive base closings but would scrap virtually no big arms programmes.
"I don't think it (base closings) is called for at this time," Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi told reporters on Monday.

But Clinton said Cohen and the military Joint Chiefs of Staff had managed their major study of force structure "brilliantly." He urged Congress to help U.S. forces retain the dominance exhibited over Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War.

"They believe it is in our national security interest and I'm going to do my best to be supportive," Clinton added during a White House photo opportunity with visiting NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.

The review plan, which requires Congressional approval, would retain the current total of about 100,000 U.S. troops in both Europe and the Western Pacific and keep the military prepared to fight two wars virtually at once, for example in the Middle East and Korea.

"If you want to keep bases, then you cannot expect to modernise," Cohen told the news conference, adding that he expected fireworks when he testified before Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday in support of the plan.
Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said base closings were preferable to deep troop cuts now.
"It would make very little sense to break the force today to pay for tomorrow's" force, he told reporters.

Closings are an explosive matter in communities that depend on local military paychecks, especially after Congress has closed dozens of small and large facilities in four previous rounds orchestrated by independent base closing and realignment commissions (BRACs).
"I know the word BRAC strikes terror in the hearts of many," said Cohen.
But he has told lawmakers the United States has too many bases now that the armed forces have already been cut by one-third since the end of the Cold War.

The QDR would reduce from 438 to 339 the planned Air Force purchase of F-22 "stealth" fighters being developed by Lockheed Martin Corp., from 1,000 to as few as 548 Navy FA-18E/F fighters built McDonnell Douglas Corp. and from 425 to 360 the number of Marine Corps' V-22 tilt-rotor helicopters being built by Boeing Co. and Textron Inc.

But it would not cancel any of those multibillion-dollar programmes and would retain long-range plans for a $170 billion joint strike fighter programme that Lockheed Martin and Boeing are competing to build in the next century.

In addition to the small active-duty force cut of 61,700, the proposal would cut 54,000 troops from part-time reserve and National Guard forces, 45,000 of those from the Army, another touchy issue with lawmakers.
Many cities and towns in the United States have reserve units, and those part-time troops depend on their paychecks for supplemental income.
Of the active-duty cuts proposed by Cohen, the Air Force would take the biggest slice with 26,900. The Navy would be reduced by 18,000, the Army by 15,000 and the Marine Corps by 1,800.
The proposal also recommended that 70,000 civilian jobs be cut from the armed forces' support network and predicted that even deeper cuts will be made in the bureaucracy following further studies.
